Orion.myth: Orion was a giant huntsman in Greek mythology. Zeus placed him among the stars after his death. The three stars of his belt are among the most recognizable patterns in the night sky.
Orion.look_here: Look for three bright stars in a straight line (the Belt). The bright orange star Betelgeuse marks his right shoulder; blue-white Rigel marks his left foot.

Ursa Major.myth: Ursa Major is the Great Bear. In Greek myth, Zeus transformed the nymph Callisto into a bear to protect her from Hera's jealousy, then placed her in the sky.
Ursa Major.look_here: Find the Big Dipper — seven bright stars forming a ladle shape. The two stars at the end of the bowl point toward Polaris, the North Star.

Ursa Minor.myth: Ursa Minor is the Little Bear. Its most famous star, Polaris, has guided travelers for millennia because it sits nearly directly above Earth's north pole.
Ursa Minor.look_here: Find Polaris at the end of the Little Dipper's handle. It stays nearly fixed while other stars wheel around it.

Cassiopeia.myth: Cassiopeia was a vain queen in Greek mythology who boasted that she was more beautiful than the sea nymphs. Poseidon punished her by tying her to a throne in the sky, doomed to circle the pole forever.
Cassiopeia.look_here: Look for a distinctive 'W' or 'M' shape of five bright stars. It's on the opposite side of Polaris from the Big Dipper.

Cygnus.myth: Cygnus is the Swan. In one myth, Zeus disguised himself as a swan. In another, the musician Orpheus was transformed into a swan after his death and placed among the stars.
Cygnus.look_here: Look for the Northern Cross — a large cross shape. The bright star Deneb marks the swan's tail; Albireo marks its beak (a beautiful blue-gold double star).

Lyra.myth: Lyra is the lyre of Orpheus, the legendary musician whose music could charm stones and soothe wild beasts. After Orpheus died, Zeus placed his lyre in the sky.
Lyra.look_here: Find bright blue-white Vega, one of the brightest stars in the sky. The lyre shape is small and compact near Vega.

Aquila.myth: Aquila is the eagle that carried Zeus's thunderbolts. It also carried Ganymede to Mount Olympus to serve as cupbearer to the gods.
Aquila.look_here: Look for Altair, a bright white star flanked by two dimmer stars (Tarazed and Alshain) — this trio is sometimes called the 'family of three.'

Scorpius.myth: Scorpius is the scorpion that killed Orion the Hunter. The gods placed both in the sky, but set them on opposite sides so they would never fight again.
Scorpius.look_here: Look for a curved 'J' shape of bright stars. The red star Antares marks the scorpion's heart. The tail curls toward the south.

Sagittarius.myth: Sagittarius is the Archer, often depicted as a centaur drawing a bow. The center of our Milky Way galaxy lies in this direction.
Sagittarius.look_here: Look for the 'Teapot' asterism — eight stars forming a teapot shape. The Milky Way appears to steam from the spout.

Leo.myth: Leo is the Nemean Lion, a beast with an impenetrable hide that Heracles (Hercules) slew as the first of his twelve labors. Zeus placed the lion in the sky to honor the feat.
Leo.look_here: Look for a backwards question mark (the Sickle) forming the lion's mane. Bright blue-white Regulus marks the lion's heart.

Taurus.myth: Taurus is the bull. Zeus transformed himself into a white bull to carry Europa across the sea. The Pleiades star cluster, within Taurus, are the seven daughters of Atlas.
Taurus.look_here: Look for the V-shaped face of the bull (the Hyades cluster) with bright orange Aldebaran as the eye. The Pleiades (Seven Sisters) are a small, fuzzy cluster nearby.

Gemini.myth: Gemini represents the twins Castor and Pollux. Castor was mortal, Pollux immortal. When Castor died, Pollux begged Zeus to let him share his immortality with his brother.
Gemini.look_here: Look for two bright stars side by side — Castor (white) and Pollux (orange). The rest of the constellation forms two stick figures.

Canis Major.myth: Canis Major is the Greater Dog, one of Orion's hunting dogs. It follows Orion across the sky through the winter months.
Canis Major.look_here: Find Sirius, the brightest star in the entire night sky. It's blue-white and twinkles fiercely when low on the horizon.

Perseus.myth: Perseus was the hero who slew Medusa and rescued Andromeda. The constellation contains the famous Double Cluster — two dense star clusters visible to the naked eye.
Perseus.look_here: Look for a curved line of stars near Cassiopeia. The Double Cluster sits between Perseus and Cassiopeia — a binocular target.

Andromeda.myth: Andromeda was a princess chained to a rock as a sacrifice to a sea monster. Perseus rescued her and married her. The constellation contains the Andromeda Galaxy, the nearest large galaxy to our own.
Andromeda.look_here: Follow the line of stars from Cassiopeia's 'W' shape outward. The Andromeda Galaxy appears as a faint, fuzzy smudge — visible to the naked eye in dark skies.

Pegasus.myth: Pegasus is the winged horse that sprang from the blood of Medusa when Perseus beheaded her. The hero Bellerophon rode Pegasus to defeat the Chimera.
Pegasus.look_here: Look for the 'Great Square' — four bright stars forming a large square. It's the body of the horse. The neck and head extend to the upper-left.

Aries.myth: Aries is the ram whose golden fleece was sought by Jason and the Argonauts. Zeus placed the ram in the sky after it was sacrificed to him.
Aries.look_here: Look for a small crooked line of three stars. Bright Hamal marks the ram's head. It's a small, faint constellation — not showy, but historically important.

Boötes.myth: Boötes is the Herdsman, the ploughman who drives the oxen of the Big Dipper around the pole. In one myth, he is Arcas, son of Zeus and Callisto.
Boötes.look_here: Find bright orange Arcturus, the brightest star in the northern sky. Follow the curve of the Big Dipper's handle to 'arc to Arcturus.' Boötes forms a kite or ice-cream-cone shape around it.

Corona Borealis.myth: Corona Borealis is the Northern Crown — the wedding crown given by Dionysus to Ariadne, daughter of King Minos of Crete, after she helped Theseus escape the labyrinth.
Corona Borealis.look_here: Look for a small semicircle of stars forming a crown shape. It sits just east of Boötes. The brightest star, Alphecca, marks the jewel in the crown.

Canes Venatici.myth: Canes Venatici represents the Hunting Dogs held on a leash by Boötes the Herdsman. They are named Asterion and Chara and help drive the bears around the pole.
Canes Venatici.look_here: Look between the handle of the Big Dipper and Boötes. It contains the Whirlpool Galaxy (M51), a beautiful face-on spiral visible in small telescopes.

Hercules.myth: Hercules (Heracles) was the greatest of Greek heroes, famous for completing twelve impossible labors. After his death, Zeus raised him to the stars as a reward for his suffering and strength.
Hercules.look_here: Look for the 'Keystone' — four stars forming a trapezoid at the center. This is Hercules's body. Inside the Keystone is M13, the Great Globular Cluster, visible in binoculars as a fuzzy ball of 300,000 stars.

Virgo.myth: Virgo is the maiden, often identified as Astraea, goddess of justice, who fled the Earth in disgust at human wickedness and was placed among the stars. She holds a sheaf of wheat marked by the bright star Spica.
Virgo.look_here: Find bright blue-white Spica, then trace the rest of the constellation sprawling to the north and west. The Virgo Cluster of galaxies lies just north of the bowl of Virgo.
